cards.claim: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is consumed first; it limits the amount of product formed.
cards.quote: the reactant, which gets consumed first, limits the amount of product formed and is, therefore, called the limiting reagent.

cards.claim: The limiting reagent is the reactant that is entirely consumed in a reaction.
cards.quote: The reactant which is entirely consumed in reaction is known as limiting reagent.

locator.section: Multiple Choice Questions (Type I), stem of Q11

cards.claim: A limiting reagent arises only when the reactants are not in the ratio the balanced equation requires; one reactant is then present in more than the required amount.
cards.quote: Many a time, reactions are carried out with the amounts of reactants that are different than the amounts as required by a balanced chemical reaction. In such situations, one reactant is in more amount than the amount required by balanced chemical reaction.

cards.claim: NCERT Problem 1.5: 50.0 kg N2 and 10.0 kg H2 are mixed to make NH3; find the amount of NH3 and identify the limiting reagent.
cards.quote: 50.0 kg of N 2 (g) and 10.0 kg of H 2 (g) are mixed to produce NH3 (g). Calculate the amount of NH3 (g) formed. Identify the limiting reagent in the production of NH3 in this situation.

cards.claim: Result of NCERT Problem 1.5: 17.86 × 10^2 mol N2 would need 5.36 × 10^3 mol H2 but only 4.96 × 10^3 mol H2 is present, so dihydrogen is the limiting reagent.
cards.quote: = 5.36 × 103 mol H2 But we have only 4.96×10 3 mol H 2. Hence, dihydrogen is the limiting reagent in this case.

cards.claim: Once the limiting reagent is used up the reaction stops, whatever the amount of the other reactant; adding more of the excess reactant does not give more product.
cards.quote: reactant which is present in the least amount gets consumed after sometime and after that further reaction does not take place whatever be the amount of the other reactant.

cards.claim: NCERT Exercise 1.23: for A + B2 -> AB2, identify the limiting reagent, if any, in five mixtures: (i) 300 atoms A + 200 molecules B, (ii) 2 mol A + 3 mol B, (iii) 100 atoms A + 100 molecules B, (iv) 5 mol A + 2.5 mol B, (v) 2.5 mol A + 5 mol B.
cards.quote: In a reaction A + B2 AB2 Identify the limiting reagent, if any, in the following reaction mixtures. (i) 300 atoms of A + 200 molecules of B (ii) 2 mol A + 3 mol B (iii) 100 atoms of A + 100 molecules of B (iv) 5 mol A + 2.5 mol B (v) 2.5 mol A + 5 mol B

question.exam: NCERT Class XI Chemistry Part I textbook exercises
question.paper: Unit 1 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry, Exercises (Reprint 2026-27)

cards.claim: NCERT answer to 1.23: (i) B is limiting, (ii) A is limiting, (iii) stoichiometric mixture, no limiting reagent, (iv) B is limiting, (v) A is limiting.
cards.quote: 1.23 (i) B is limiting (ii) A is limiting (iii) Stoichiometric mixture –No (iv) B is limiting (v) A is limiting

locator.section: Answers to Some Selected Problems, Unit 1

cards.claim: NCERT Exemplar 1.35 (short answer): in 2A + 4B -> 3C + 4D, 5 mol A react with 6 mol B; which is the limiting reagent and how much C forms?
cards.quote: The reactant which is entirely consumed in reaction is known as limiting reagent. In the reaction 2A + 4B → 3C + 4D, when 5 moles of A react with 6 moles of B, then (i) which is the limiting reagent? (ii) calculate the amount of C formed?

question.exam: NCERT Exemplar Problems Chemistry Class XI
question.paper: Unit 1 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry (2025-26 edition)

cards.claim: NCERT Exemplar answer to 35: 5 mol A would need 10 mol B, but only 6 mol B is present, so B is the limiting reagent; 6 mol B gives 4.5 mol of C.
cards.quote: But we have only 6 mols of ‘B’, hence, ‘B’ is the limiting reagent. So amount of ‘C’ formed is determined by amount of ‘B’. Since 4 mols of ‘B’ give 3 mols of ‘C’. Hence 6 mols of ‘B’ will give 3 mol of C6 mol of B × 4 mol of B = 4.5 mol of C

cards.claim: NCERT Exemplar 1.43 (long answer): what mass of CaCl2 forms when 250 mL of 0.76 M HCl reacts with 1000 g of CaCO3? Name the limiting reagent and find the moles of CaCl2.
cards.quote: What mass of CaCl2 will be formed when 250 mL of 0.76 M HCl reacts with 1000 g of CaCO3? Name the limiting reagent. Calculate the number of moles of CaCl2 formed in the reaction.

question.exam: NCERT Exemplar Problems Chemistry Class XI
question.paper: Unit 1 Some Basic Concepts of Chemistry (2025-26 edition)

cards.claim: NCERT Exemplar answer to 43 (first part): only 0.19 mol HCl is available, so HCl is the limiting reagent and fixes the amount of CaCl2 formed.
cards.quote: But we have only 0.19 mol HCl (aq), hence, HCl (aq) is limiting reagent. So amount of CaCl2 formed will depend on the amount of HCl available.

cards.claim: NCERT Exemplar answer to 43 (continued): 0.19 mol HCl gives 0.095 mol CaCl2, i.e. 0.095 × 111 = 10.54 g.
cards.quote: would give: 0.19 mol HCl (aq) × 21 mol CaCl (aq) 2 mol HCl (aq) = 0.095 mol or 0.095 × molar mass of CaCl2 = 0.095 × 111 = 10.54 g
